lessons.title: Free-running, locked, and scheduled phases
lessons.physicalIntuition: Independent comparators may request pulses at inconvenient times. Coordination can align, defer, or choose phases, trading immediate voltage response against ripple cancellation and fairness.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Define per-phase request guards and a scheduler grant function constrained by eligibility, phase state, and minimum separation. Fixed-spacing locking adds phase-error dynamics; free-running behavior is measured statistically rather than assumed periodic.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Implement selectable educational schedulers—ideal spacing, first eligible, round robin, minimum separation, current priority, and simplified free running—with request/grant/deny logs.
lessons.transferQuestion: When would immediate first-eligible grants improve voltage response but worsen output ripple?

lessons.title: Collisions, bunching, beats, starvation, and fairness
lessons.physicalIntuition: Too-close pulses add current slope together; nearly equal free-running frequencies drift in and out of alignment; a greedy scheduler can repeatedly deny one phase.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Define collision as separation below a chosen threshold, bunching by clustered inter-grant intervals, beat signatures from phase-difference drift, starvation by maximum denial/age, and fairness by normalized grant counts or wait times over a stated window.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Metrics include observation window, eligible-request denominator, and per-phase frequency distribution. Minimum-separation denial must create a visible delayed or dropped request.
assumptions: fairness metric is a declared modeling choice
lessons.transferQuestion: Design a request sequence that starves phase 3 under a naive current-priority rule and repair the rule.

lessons.title: Current-balance loops and loop interaction
lessons.physicalIntuition: A balance loop nudges per-phase demand or timing so one phase does not carry excess current. If it reacts as fast as the main regulator, both loops may fight over the same transient.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Compute each phase's selected current metric relative to the phase average and pass the error through a bandwidth-limited balance compensator. Analyze coupled small-signal paths qualitatively or with a multi-input model; bandwidth separation is a design choice, not a universal ratio.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The current web challenge displays actual and sensed current trajectories, estimated per-phase peaks, every balance trim, RMS sharing error, normalized primary/share bandwidth references, and a disclosed voltage-interaction proxy. Full voltage commands, coupled multi-input Bode responses, saturation, and total-command conservation remain capstone validation tasks.
lessons.transferQuestion: What waveform evidence suggests the current-share loop is competing with the voltage loop?

lessons.title: Large steps, priority, phase shedding, and re-entry
lessons.physicalIntuition: A large step asks for pulses now, but granting all phases simultaneously sacrifices spacing and can hit limits. Scheduler policy chooses where the stress and droop appear.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Constrain grants by phase current limit, one-shot/min-off timers, separation, and active-phase set. Compare round-robin fairness with current-priority error reduction and add aging/fairness terms to prevent starvation.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The scheduler lab compares request/grant/drop timing, collisions, delay, allocation fairness, service fairness, a disabled phase, inhibited requests, and timed re-entry. Voltage droop, per-phase current-limit dynamics, threshold hysteresis, soft current handoff, and large-step recovery remain separate PSpice capstone benches rather than outputs of this scheduler-only model.
lessons.interaction: Exercise scheduler deadline and phase-re-entry policies, then design a large-step pulse-allocation tournament as a PSpice capstone scenario
lessons.transferQuestion: Which constraint would you relax first for a severe load step, and what new failure mode appears?
